Document evidence:
[S1] 1 Motivation (p.1–1)
The Cedar pilot examined greenhouse water use by comparing a timer‑based irrigation schedule with a moisture‑sensor schedule over fourteen days under identical greenhouse conditions. Six trays per schedule, using the same soil and seedlings, were irrigated daily; irrigation volume was recorded each day and plant height measured at the study’s end. The aim was to reduce unnecessary irrigation while maintaining growth. The same caretaker inspected both groups each morning, and any equipment failures were logged before daily totals were calculated. The study is a small descriptive pilot, not intended to generalize to outdoor farms or long‑term crop yields.

[S2] 2 Timer Results (p.2–2)
The timer schedule irrigated 42 L total across six trays over a fourteen‑day pilot, running at fixed intervals regardless of soil moisture; daily logs noted some watering when soil was already moist, but no timer failures occurred. The timer group’s mean final plant height was 18 cm. No variance estimates or significance tests were reported. Authors suggest future work test different soils, larger groups, and longer periods.

[S3] 3 Sensor Results (p.3–3)
The sensor schedule delivered 30 L of water across six trays in a fourteen‑day pilot. Mean final plant height was 19 cm. Irrigation was triggered when moisture fell below the configured threshold; one loose cable was repaired before day 1 and no failures occurred. The pilot observed lower total water use with the sensor schedule while achieving a similar final plant height. Authors note the report does not establish causality or long‑term yield, limit findings to the tested trays and conditions, and recommend a larger controlled trial, further threshold calibration, and sensor maintenance study.
